This question has two parts that apply to my relationship.

  1. My SO has a crush on someone, is interested in pursuing a friendship, and says they don't intend to act on the crush.
  2. Someone I work with has an unreciprocated crush on me and I'd really love to be friends and activity partners with them.

In both cases, if single we'd pursue more than friendship with the other person.

Is it appropriate in the context of a monogamous long term relationship to go after these friendships? I'd thought no and had initially put distance between my coworker and I. My partner thinks theirs is okay though and I feel like mine is more monogamous than that.

If it's relevant, we recently nearly split up and this situation and opinions span that incident unchanged.

I should also mention that I don't really understand crushes. I've either wanted someone and pursued them or had no interest. It seems odd to me to have a crush while in a relationship but I understand it's apparently pretty normal.
LTRs and crushes. Can you be friends?

All of the crushes I've had while in a LTR have eventually, one way or another, become more than that. Either within the span of the relationship or directly following it. I think disallowing the friendship is a bad move, because it will likely drive your SO away, but I don't think getting closer to someone you have a crush on is the right thing for your SO to do.

Your situation is a little different, since they have a crush on you that you don't reciprocate, but it's still not much different. I'd just shy away from crushes and I'd want my SO to do the same.

Thanks for taking the time to reply. That basically matches what I was thinking. While the whole crush thing isn't really intuitive for me, it seems counter-intuitive to foster relationships where a crush is involved if you don't want a romantic or sexual component to develop. I also agree with you that partners really shouldn't be disallowing things like this though.

On the other hand, my SO doesn't have many friends and is pretty lonely so if someone is appealing for friendship, do you think it's more reasonable for them to pursue that friendship in spite of a crush?

Likewise in my case, I think I could be best of friends with this person I know. Do the higher rewards affect it at all?

It depends on what you and your relationship is comfortable with I think. It's going to take a lot of open communication, you need to know you can trust your SO. The last thing your relationship needs after a recent split is any kind of sneaking or hiding, or even feelings of suspected sneaking or hiding. If the friendships do move forward, I think the two friends need to meet the SO's and respect the both of you on the relationship. Have you met your SO's crush? Do they seem trustworthy, or do they seem like the type who would steal your SO if they realized there were feelings involved?

Also, Idk the genders involved here, but if the friendships/crushes are same gender as the associated relationship person, that's a little more innocent I think. If your girl has got a crush on a guy, my personal bias is that she'll end up persuing him (even if she doesn't realize she's doing it).

I understand the appeal of friends. Friends are awesome. The thing you have to be careful of is the fact that you could be best of friends with that other person. Could you be better friends with them then you are with your SO? Could they, also? Lifelong relationships are built on a bond of friendship. My current long term relationship came out of my long term best friend (he's a guy, I'm a girl). Even though I reassured my other boyfriends that he wasn't a threat.

Honestly? (Take this with a grain of salt because it's totally opinion) I think that you should pursue the friendships. Based solely on what you've said about you two, you had a recent split and that issue is still there. Maybe you're not meant to be. Maybe these friends and crushes are here for a reason.

Sorry for the huge wall of text. I love relationships stuff. I could do more with your genders/ages/relationship length and living situation.

I don't reveal my own sex or orientation on this account for privacy and to avoid stereotypes (I prefer my posts to be judged purely on content) but I'll tell you some more about the situation.

My SO and I between 25 and 30, own a home together, are raising children, consider ourselves life partners, and have been together for 7 years. All sexes and orientations are such that those being crushed on could theoretically reciprocate. To clarify too, we only nearly spilt.

My SO and I have never met the other people involved. I've told my SO a lot about my friend/coworker because we sat together at work and I always was hearing great/crazy/funny stories that I wanted to share. My SO really likes the sound of my friend.

I know very little about my SO's crush; nothing about character and just a little about their accomplishments. They sound like a decent and respectable person. My SO used to go to school with them and has recently gotten back in touch on Facebook.

I trust my SO to be completely honest and faithful. I'd say probability of an affair is basically zero. They could certainly fall for someone else and lose interest though. That's my only worry about them pursuing this friendship.

I definitely think that your situation is more stable than, say, two 16 year olds in high school having this issue. In some ways it's better, in some it's worse.

You know your partner and your situation better than anyone else, though. All I can say is I'd probably feel weird if my SO and I were in your situation, and he felt it was appropriate to develop this outside relationship, especially from Facebook and with a crush involved, I'd be hurt and confused. Owning a home and raising kids is a time consuming business, and so is a marriage/LTR like yours. I mean, your SO wants to devote precious time and energy that could go into the family into her crush... That's a little weird.

Communicate and meet their friend. And fix the nearly split issue... Otherwise, yeah, you're right they'll get disinterested and leave.

I don't think it's weird for my SO to want to invest a little time doing something other than family/us. It's definitely important to be your own person and make time for hobbies/friends. Neither my SO or I has done well making enough time for that.

That said, it seems odd that they'd invest in someone they have a crush on, but I don't want to be controlling or distrustful.

Is that really so different than me wanting to make friends with someone who likes me and with whom I'd pursue a relationship if single?

I do think there's some value in meeting these people though, so thanks for that suggestion.

I do not have experience on the matter...

But if you allow your SO to develop feelings for someone, it will inevitably follow that they will compare you to them. I think that would be dangerous in a long term relationship, as there will be periods of drought in the relationship where things aren't going a 100%. That's natural. However, its not going to help the relationship if within those periods of drought your SO is comparing you to someone they both glamorize and (as is often the cases with crushes) willing to overlook any faults that person may have.

My SO thinks their crush will atrophy in friendship, mostly due to the loss of glamorization you mention. Having never crushed on anyone, I don't know how psychologically realistic that is. I'd have guessed it would get worse, but what do I know?

You say that if I allow my SO to develop feelings for someone, there might be trouble. I don't see how I can allow or disallow it though. Isn't that out of my hands?

Yes, it is out of your hands. "Allow" isn't the right word then.

How serious is this "crush"? When I have a "crush" on someone, I make a commitment to liking them and will purposely overlook their flaws. I put quotations marks around "crush" because that's not how I would describe it. A crush is someone I would like to pursue, that I like, and there is a purpose to thinking about them. But it's very possible that your SO's "crush" is just an innocent affection they have. To be honest, I don't know if having affections for others is the right thing to do in a LTR as it's never come up as an issue in my relationships.

Since it is out of your hands, I think the best thing you can do is trust your SO. Distrusting them will only hurt the relationship, and trusting them washes your hands of the situation (if things go sour you can say you did everything you could to keep the relationship solid, including not pushing them away and trusting them).

I think its a good thing that your SO would tell you about their crush.

I agree that it's a good thing. My SO is extremely honest and I can't imagine them lying.

You bring up a good point too: what the heck is a crush exactly? I should just ask what they mean. I took it to mean they're interested in dating the person and forming a LTR with them. That's why I say my friend's crush is unreciprocated. If a crush just means you think someone looks nice and find them desirable from a looks/personality/interests standpoint, then I have a crush on my friend too. I just never thought of the word that way. Thanks for raising that issue. I'd just been assuming since vague meaning.

It probably depends on the people involved. Does your SO's crush have feelings for them? If not, I don't think it makes much sense to end the friendship. Do they spend time in person, or just contact each other online? You mention your SO is lonely. Maybe there are some same sex people at their workplace they could make friends with. I read another thread of yours, OP, and you mentioned being in a 2 year friendship with someone your SO didn't like, and then the friend came to your workplace. And now someone at work has a crush on you? Same person?

I don't know how my SO's crush feels. I've never met them. So far they just interact online but my SO wants to get together in person. My SO is both lonely and picky. It's rare that find someone they want to be friends with.

That former friend of mine you mention has (fortunately) seemed to have lost all interest. A couple people at work out of dozens there that are attracted to my sex have obvious crushes on me. One is in another department, I rarely see, and have no interest in befriending. So that situation is easy. The other coworker is in my department, interacts with me regularly, and I very much would like to be friends. I really think I could be besties with them. On this front I'm worried that my SO could get upset (they say they don't mind though) or that I could be unsuccessful in fostering a good friendship because the crush gets in the way.

Chances are the crush doesn't feel the same way. I've found that most crushes are not reciprocated. How do you feel about your SO meeting their crush in person vs. online? Do you think SO can keep from acting on the crush? It sounds like you and SO have some issues with crushes going on, both on you, and on other people. How does SO feel about you feeling like best friends with the person at work? Have you and your SO ever considered being in an open relationship? It sounds like you've got a lot going on to work through, but thinking about that 2 year thing, I wonder if your SO is trying to find something like that too.

I have complete confidence my SO wouldn't cheat even if the interest was reciprocated. They've got way too much integrity for that. Entirely possible they could lose interest and decide to leave me though. I don't have any idea how likely something like that is since I don't really understand what it's like to have a crush.

I don't really have any feelings about them associating with someone (online or in person) that they have a crush on other than feeling a little upset that I got in trouble for perceived non-monogamy with that school friend when this feels similar, though far less serious. I guess I'm a touch upset about what seems like a tiny bit of hypocrisy but I think I may be overreacting; crushes may just be more normal/harmless than I think.

When you talk about having issues with crushes you make such things sound uncommon. Is it unusual for people in relationships to be either crushing or the object of a crush? I really don't know how normal this is. I've usually had one or two people showing an obvious interest at school/university so my situation at work doesn't strike me as particularly odd. Neither person is behaving unprofessionally (well, the one I want to befriend, R, said I'm exactly like J, right after telling me how they wanted to sleep with or even marry J).

To clarify, when I say best friends, I still would be closer friends with my SO. I'm just saying that I could see myself being close friends with R forever to distinguish it from someone I just hang out with a bit. My SO has a positive attitude towards R and thinks R's comments are just due to them being a little awkward. J had been R's best friend, making the comment above possibly less creepy. Me, my SO, and R share so many unusual values and interests we all have speculated we'd make good friends.

As for an open relationship, my SO is pretty much religiously monogamous (metaphorically; we're atheists). I have no interest in one either because it sounds like too much hassle and drama; one is almost more than enough for me. :-)

Your last point is interesting speculation. It's certainly possible. I recently admitted to my SO and myself that I was having an emotional affair with school friend. While I didn't want anything romantic or sexual, I really enjoyed having someone basically worship the ground I walked on while my SO and I were going through a rough patch. Maybe they're seeking some cheap positive attention since we're stressed while working out the issues caused by my affair.

I think it's a little odd to have so many crushes/potential relationships when you're in a LTR. I'm not sure that I see the similarity between your 2 year long emotional affair and your SO's crush/communication online. Is your SO saying anything inappropriate to their crush? Has your SO ever cheated? You've mentioned that your partner doesn't have many friends (picky), could it be that this really is just a friendship?

I hesitate to say that it's wrong to have crush friends in a LTR, but I think you do have to be cautious. Maintain good communication with your partner. I would be careful how you talk about this issue too, because if your partner doesn't have many friends, they might feel like you are trying to limit their social options.

As for my affair vs my partner's crush, I don't think they're really equivalent at all. My partner has never cheated or said anything inappropriate. I think they do just want a friend.

Thanks for the communication tips. I don't want my SO to feel like I'm trying to limit their friendships. I think all things considered, their crush sounds harmless and it seems totally reasonable for them to want to be friends with this person.

Do you think I should pursue a friendship with R? Any additional context needed for an answer?

Glad you have that worked out. I hope you and your SO can work things out and be happy.

It's kind of strange that R compared you to J, someone they wanted to marry. Do you know in what way they thought you were the same (no need to specify)? I would be a little concerned that R is transferring feelings for someone else on to you. You might want to take it slow, and make your exact intent known. If it is going to be just a friendship, make sure R knows that. You don't want it to be an unpleasant surprise a few months in.

Thanks for the kind wishes and assistance getting to a good resolution. Talking with you helped me see things from my SO's point of view more and made be take a second look at how reasonable my objections were.

R was talking with me about their life and experiences in college and told me about how much they'd cared for J. J couldn't reciprocate due to religious differences (J: Mormon, R: atheist) but they stayed close friends. R mentioned with regret that J wouldn't share their bed or consider marriage because of that.

As we were getting to know each other, R commented that R and I were very similar. I was surprised because I didn't see it yet and (much later) when I realized they'd been right I asked how they could tell so early. They replied that I was basically exactly like J in every way so they'd guessed more of my personality than our limited conversations at that time would have let on.

That's why I worry about transference and suspect it's the basis for (or at least component of) the crush. I actually bet getting to know me better would help reduce that transference as I became more of a distinct individual to R.

In theory I like establishing intentions and boundaries like you're talking about. Just coming up to R and asking to go on bike rides, hikes, or shooting could be ambiguous and interpreted as a bit of a date (and I really have no idea of their feelings about adultery or non-monogamy, so they could be excited at the prospect for all I know). In practice, I don't know how to approach a coworker and be like "want to go hang out this weekend (no amore)?". That sounds awkward as hell and pretty unprofessional. Did you have a method in mind? I'd also be interested in how one takes a friendship slow. I had just planned on proposing activities of mutual interest together outside of work or having lunch together at work to talk more. I tend to make fast friends and I'm not sure what going slow looks like. Heck, once I met a nice couple in a hostel over the weekend and scored an invite back to their home in a different country. I ended up visiting them for a week and have stayed in touch ever since. R is similar in this regard too.

I think my main worry here is that R will get the wrong idea and end up getting hurt or it spoiling the friendship. I'd be very surprised if they made inappropriate advances like my school friend did and caused trouble with my SO. R is a fairly gentle and passive person whereas that school person was rather assertive and manipulative.
